title: Vectorization
sub: How Burst handles 4–8 numbers with one instruction, and what gets in its way
cards/0/body:
The main reason Burst is fast on number crunching is SIMD (single instruction, multiple data). A CPU register holds several numbers instead of one, and a single instruction processes all of them at once.

SSE has 128-bit xmm registers, which is 4 floats. AVX/AVX2 has 256-bit ymm registers, 8 floats. ARM has NEON, 128 bits. The instruction sets to build for are chosen in the Burst AOT settings; if you pick several (on Windows, macOS, Linux and Android), Burst puts several variants of the code into the build and picks the one that fits the CPU at startup.

The usual road to SIMD is loop auto-vectorization: LLVM takes several iterations and turns them into one instruction. You write a plain for, and the assembly shows a vmulps doing 8 numbers. The same holds inside IJobParallelFor and IJobFor with ScheduleParallel: Burst compiles Execute together with the loop each worker runs over its batch of indices, usually inlines Execute into that loop, and can vectorize it. But only if the body meets the conditions.
cards/1/body:
The compiler merges iterations only if that doesn’t change the result. Hence the conditions:

Iterations are independent. a[i] = a[i - 1] * 0.5f can’t be merged: every step waits for the previous one.

The trip count is known on entry. A break or return in the middle, and in the Burst manual’s example the loop turns scalar.

Memory is contiguous. a[i], a[i + 1]… load with one instruction. If the fields are scattered across structs, the numbers have to be gathered one by one (that’s the SoA lesson).

Writes don’t overlap reads — that’s aliasing, next card.

A float sum is a dependency too. Vectorizing it means reordering the additions, and with the default FloatMode (Strict) Burst doesn’t do that. More in the determinism lesson.
cards/2/q: Which loop in a Burst job vectorizes (fields are NativeArray<float>, default FloatMode)?
cards/2/options/3: for (i…) total += a[i];   // total is a float
cards/2/explain: The iterations are independent, the memory is contiguous and there is no early exit, so the square root and the multiply become sqrtps and mulps on several numbers at a time. break makes the trip count unknown, a[i - 1] depends on the previous step, and a float sum needs the additions reordered, which Strict doesn’t allow.
cards/2/wrong/1: A break in the middle: the compiler doesn’t know how many iterations will run, so the loop stays scalar.
cards/2/wrong/2: Each iteration reads what the previous one wrote. That’s a prefix sum, and it can’t be merged into one instruction.
cards/2/wrong/3: A vector sum is 8 partial sums added up at the end, which is a different order of additions. In Strict mode Burst doesn’t change the order.
cards/3/body:
Aliasing is when two pointers look at overlapping memory. If dst may equal src + 1, writing dst[i] changes src[i + 1], and processing 8 elements at once is no longer valid. A compiler that isn’t sure has to go one by one, or insert an overlap check before the loop and keep a scalar fallback — extra code and extra comparisons.

In a job this is solved for you: the job struct and its container fields (NativeArray, NativeSlice) are treated as non-overlapping by default. That is why a plain loop in a job vectorizes “for free”. The exception is a field marked [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction]: Burst assumes it may overlap the others.

In a static method on pointers you make the promise yourself: [NoAlias] on a parameter means “doesn’t overlap the other parameters”. Nobody checks the promise: if the memory does overlap, you get undefined behaviour and very nasty bugs. Different element types don’t save you from aliasing either: in C#, Burst draws no such conclusion.
cards/4/q: What is true about aliasing in Burst? Pick all that apply.
cards/4/options/0: NativeArray fields of a job struct are treated as non-overlapping by default
cards/4/options/1: Burst treats a field marked [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] as possibly overlapping the others
cards/4/options/2: If you put [NoAlias] on pointers that actually overlap, Burst detects it and throws an exception
cards/4/options/3: A NativeArray<byte> and a NativeArray<float> can’t overlap because their types differ
cards/4/explain: Burst treats the containers of a job as non-overlapping by default — that’s why loops in jobs vectorize so well. [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] removes that guarantee too. [NoAlias] is a promise, not a check: a false promise is undefined behaviour. And Burst doesn’t reason “different types, different memory”: in C# a byte pointer can point where a float pointer does.
cards/5/body:
A SIMD instruction takes 8 numbers down one path. If each element has its own if, the 8 “lanes” may want different paths, and you can’t jump. The compiler has to turn the branch into a masked choice or leave the loop scalar. LLVM rewrites simple cases on its own: an if whose two branches cheaply write to the same place often becomes a select by itself. But not always: a write in only one branch, a long body, a call — and the loop stays scalar.

math.select(a, b, c) from Unity.Mathematics makes the choice explicit: it returns b if c is true, otherwise a. Both sides are computed up front and a mask picks one — no jump, and no hoping the optimizer spots the pattern by itself. There are overloads for float4 with bool4, where the choice is made per lane.

The price is that both sides get computed. For cheap expressions that’s nothing; for heavy ones (a call, a loop) it isn’t. For the common cases there are ready-made branch-free functions: math.min, math.max, math.clamp, math.abs.
cards/6/q: Build the line without a branch: if the speed is above maxSpeed, take maxSpeed, otherwise the speed itself.
cards/6/explain: math.select(ifFalse, ifTrue, condition): when s > maxSpeed it returns the second argument, maxSpeed, otherwise the first, s. The short way to write the same thing is math.min(s, maxSpeed).
cards/7/body:
Whether a loop vectorized is not something you guess — you look. Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector, pick the job under Compile Targets on the left, and the Assembly view on the right.

You don’t need to read all of it. Find the body of the hot loop and look at the instruction suffix: ss is scalar single, one number (mulss, addss); ps is packed single, the whole register (mulps, addps). The v prefix is just the AVX encoding: vmulss is still one number. ymm registers hold 8 floats, xmm hold 4 or one.

The Highlight SIMD Scalar vs Packed option helps: it colours scalar and packed instructions differently. If the loop didn’t vectorize, the LLVM IR Optimization Diagnostics view tells you what got in the way.

There is also a compile-time check: Loop.ExpectVectorized() from Unity.Burst.CompilerServices gives error BC1321 if the loop isn’t vectorized. It is experimental — it needs the UNITY_BURST_EXPERIMENTAL_LOOP_INTRINSICS define — and it doesn’t work inside an if.
cards/8/q: In the Burst Inspector the body of the hot loop looks like this. What does it mean?
cards/8/options/0: The loop isn’t vectorized: vmulss multiplies one number per iteration, even though it’s an AVX-encoded instruction
cards/8/options/1: The loop is vectorized for AVX: the v prefix and xmm registers mean 4 numbers at a time
cards/8/options/2: Burst is off, and this is Mono code
cards/8/options/3: Safety checks are on; without them the code would be packed
cards/8/explain: The ss suffix is scalar single: one number. The v prefix is only the AVX encoding, and xmm is used for a single lane here. On every iteration rax grows by 1 — one element. Next stop: LLVM IR Optimization Diagnostics, to see what got in the way, aliasing or a branch.
cards/8/wrong/1: The vector version would be vmulps (packed), and the counter would grow by 4 or 8. Here it’s ss and inc rax.
cards/8/wrong/2: The Inspector’s Assembly view shows the code Burst compiled, not Mono.
cards/8/wrong/3: Checks add comparisons and calls, but the ss suffix is about a scalar instruction, not about checks.
cards/9/task: Remove the branch from DamageJob: Execute must compute the result with math.select (add Unity.Mathematics), with no if. If the damage is greater than or equal to the health, the result is 0, otherwise hp − damage. Keep the [BurstCompile] attribute.
cards/9/checks/3/label: The result is written to result[i]
cards/9/explain: Both sides — 0 and hp − damage — are cheap, so computing both and picking with a mask beats a jump, and the IJobFor loop stays vectorizable. LLVM would often turn a simple if like this one, where both branches write result[i], into a select on its own, but math.select makes it explicit and doesn’t depend on the optimizer’s luck. math.max(0f, hp[i] - damage[i]) would work here too. In the interview: “I take branches out of the hot loop with math.select or min/max and check in the Burst Inspector that the instructions are packed.”
cards/10/q: Interviewer: “The same loop over NativeArray in a job compiles to a clean vector loop, but in a static Burst method on pointers the Inspector shows extra code: an overlap check on entry and a scalar fallback loop. Why, and what do you do?”
cards/10/options/0: Burst doesn’t know that dst and src don’t overlap; I promise it with [NoAlias] on the parameters and check in the Inspector
cards/10/options/1: Burst never vectorizes static methods, so I move the code into a job
cards/10/options/2: The k parameter is the problem; it should be a field
cards/10/options/3: Pointers are banned in Burst, so I replace them with NativeArray
cards/10/explain: A job’s container fields are NoAlias by default, but the compiler knows nothing about two raw pointers: dst may equal src + 1. So it checks for overlap on entry and keeps a scalar fallback, or at worst leaves the loop scalar. [NoAlias] settles the question — provided you really guarantee the memory doesn’t overlap.
cards/10/wrong/1: Static [BurstCompile] methods are compiled by the same Burst and vectorize by the same rules.
cards/10/wrong/2: The scalar k is the same for every iteration and gets in nobody’s way.
cards/10/wrong/3: Pointers and unsafe code are allowed in Burst.
